papers.title: On Higher-Form Fracton Hydrodynamics with Momentum Conservation
papers.summary: Momentum conservation is common in fluids, yet it may be incompatible with the hydrodynamics of theories with exotic conservation laws (such as fracton hydrodynamics) unless symmetries are spontaneously broken. Using the Martin-Siggia-Rose (MSR) effective field theory formalism, we develop a representation-theoretic framework for the hydrodynamics of translationally invariant systems with exotic conservation laws without spontaneous symmetry breaking. Under mild assumptions on the form of hydrodynamics, we show that such theories must satisfy two representation theoretic consistency conditions and a generalized Gauss's law constraint. Higher-form symmetries satisfy these conditions and we derive their ideal hydrodynamics; in three dimensions, the one-form case produces ideal non-relativistic magnetohydrodynamics. Finally, we prove that no other theories are compatible with momentum conservation in SO(3) nor SO($d$), for sufficiently large odd $d$.

papers.title: Boundary-Sensitive Quantum Order on Non-Amenable Lattices
papers.summary: We show that quantum systems on non-amenable lattices, whose boundaries constitute an extensive fraction of the system, host novel forms of bulk ordering with no Euclidean counterpart. Combining boundary-retaining iDMRG with an exact symmetry-fixing duality, we investigate $p<5$ state clock models on the coordination-3 infinite Cayley tree. We find that between the ordered and disordered phases lies an emergent intermediate phase with bulk order induced by an arbitrarily weak boundary field rather than by conventional spontaneous symmetry-breaking. This establishes boundary-sensitive order as a distinct quantum ordering mechanism defying Landau's spontaneous symmetry-breaking paradigm. The intermediate phase realizes a bulk-boundary correspondence in which the unpolarized boundary selects a specific ordered bulk state.

papers.title: Field theory guides Monte Carlo in the one-dimensional long-range Ising model
papers.summary: The statistical long-range Ising (LRI) model in one dimension provides a family of some of the simplest non-exactly solvable critical points. These critical points are described by long-range conformal field theories (CFTs) that are well understood analytically with perturbative expansions and some exact results. Guided by this, we revisit the Monte Carlo (MC) approach to the corresponding lattice model which has many favorable features compared to other systems studied with MC methods. In particular, with very modest computational cost, we are able to estimate scaling dimensions of leading and subleading operators as well as the associated three-point functions, and even certain four-point functions. These results help highlight the fact that 1d LRI CFTs are a phenomenal playground to more generally test non-perturbative methods and ideas for strongly coupled CFTs.

papers.title: A McLennan formula for equiaccessible steady states
papers.summary: Near equilibrium, the Boltzmann distribution is corrected by the transient irreversible entropy flux, a result known as the McLennan formula. By expanding around equiaccessible steady states instead, we derive an analogue that can hold arbitrarily far from equilibrium. At zeroth order, steady-state occupation is determined solely by local escape rates, yielding a strong form of the active-matter principle of "low rattling." The first-order correction measures the impact of traffic imbalances on the accessibility of each state, marking the onset of nonlocal determinants of relative occupation.

papers.title: Phase-sensitive quantum-state texture during thermalization of a Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya Heisenberg dimer
papers.summary: We investigate quantum-state texture during the thermal relaxation of an anisotropic spin-$1/2$ Heisenberg dimer subject to a longitudinal magnetic field and a Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) interaction. Starting from local transverse and longitudinal couplings to a bosonic bath, we construct a global weak-coupling Lindblad equation, identify its transition channels, and discuss the applicability and limitations of the secular approximation. The Gibbs state is obtained explicitly in the local spin basis, revealing that the DM coupling controls both the modulus and phase of the single-excitation coherence by modifying the energy splitting and rotating the chiral phase. For heating and cooling protocols, we compare rugosity, fidelity-based texture, and trace-distance texture with coherence, vector spin chirality, and purity. The relaxation dynamics separates population thermalization from the decay and precession of deliberately prepared energy-basis coherence. Their combined contribution to local coherence produces DM-dependent texture overshoots and, during cooling, damped oscillations and sign changes of the coherence quadratures. These transients differ from the evolution of coherence magnitude and purity, while trace-distance texture weights them differently from the overlap-based quantifiers. Calculations at reduced dissipation preserve the texture maxima within the secular model. The results identify a phase-sensitive diagnostic of relaxation.

papers.title: Dynamic clustering of active chemotactic Janus particles
papers.summary: Modeling self-propulsion as an emergent diffusiophoretic effect, we come back to the dynamic clustering experiment of active Janus colloids. Working in the original three-dimensional geometry, and using the chemical solute concentration as a control parameter, we find that the dynamic clustering region occupies a robust fraction of the phase diagram. This behavior is rationalized using a linear stability analysis that efficiently captures the instability of the gas phase to dynamic clusters. We also find that dynamic clustering results from the combined effects of a Keller-Segel collapse and of a motility-induced phase separation, either being arrested by the orientational coupling to the chemical field in agreement with previous work.

papers.title: Nucleation-type criticality with infinite number of free-energy minima beyond mean-field theory
papers.summary: We study the phase diagram of a three-dimensional Heisenberg model with Dzyaloshinski--Moriya interaction under the presence of Potts-like anisotropy. The phase transition between the winding phase and the ferromagnetically ordered phase exhibits a critical phase transition with anomalous features such as critical exponents consistent with that of a first-order transition while maintaining continuity of physical quantities. Furthermore, at the critical point, we see a growing number of free energy local minima, supporting the picture of infinitely many discontinuous transitions forming criticality. Our numerical result unify de Gennes' theory of nucleation-type transitions and Dzyaloshinskii's calculation of chiral magnets by demonstrating that such anomalous criticality can be realized in microscopic models beyond mean-field.

papers.title: Statistical decision theory in thermodynamics
papers.summary: We introduce statistical decision theory in stochastic thermodynamic systems. Statistical decision theory integrates several statistical tasks, such as estimation, hypothesis testing, and classification. In this study, we consider statistical decision theory in stochastic thermodynamics, which unifies sensing, classification, and uncertainty relations. In particular, we focus on the minimax risk, the smallest achievable expected loss under the worst-case parameter choice, even with an optimal estimator. We derive lower bounds on the minimax risk using Le Cam's two-point method. The derived relationships can be used across a broader range of thermodynamic scenarios. To illustrate these relations, we study classification and distribution estimation problems in a Markov process. We demonstrate that the minimax risk provides lower bounds given by the dynamical activity in these problems. Furthermore, by examining particular dynamics, we establish that the resulting bounds simplify to uncertainty relations involving dynamical activity or entropy production.

papers.title: From particles to continuum theories in effective models of self-propelled rods
papers.summary: Models of colliding self-propelled rods are abstractions of many real systems such as gliding bacteria and biofilaments displaced by molecular motors. They have been studied mostly in two space dimensions and shown to display a wealth of different collective regimes with many parameters involved in the ensuing phase diagrams. Continuum-level theories faithful to this phenomenology are largely lacking since coarse-graining models of explicit rods is notoriously difficult. Here we study collections of particles in which the rods geometry is taken into account effectively, by implementing the nematic alignment of their velocities and two types of repulsion. These Vicsek-style models are simple enough to be starting points for systematic coarse-graining. We thus derive hydrodynamic equations that we show to have solutions qualitatively faithful to their particle-level origin.

papers.title: Avalanches and Aging Driven by Parametric Amplification in Kerr Oscillator Networks
papers.summary: Gain, loss, and nonlinearity shape the phase-space landscape of driven-dissipative systems, such as Kerr parametric oscillator (KPO) networks realized in superconducting, nanomechanical, and photonic arrays. Networks of KPOs exploit the stationary states of this landscape for Ising machines, bosonic error-correcting codes, and sensing. Yet how transients reach these states from a given initial condition remains largely unexplored. Here we show that KPO networks with nonlinear couplings can develop avalanches in their transient dynamics: rapid cascades of amplification between modes reminiscent of the relaxation avalanches of glassy systems. The mechanism is that parametric gain first activates the modes whose detuning it can overcome, and their nonlinear frequency shifts then pull dormant modes into the gain window one at a time. Dormant modes keep decaying while they wait for their turn, so every activation starts from a smaller seed and the intervals between activations grow geometrically. The network thus ages: the longer it has evolved, the slower it changes, and activations accumulate only logarithmically in time. In a 20-mode network, each dwell lasts about twice as long as the previous one. While aging delays the approach to the stationary state, additive noise sets a floor on the seeds and unsticks the network, shortening the longest dwells first while the activation sequence survives to noise several orders of magnitude stronger.

papers.title: Phase Diagram of the Two-Dimensional Vicsek Model
papers.summary: Motivated by gaps in our current knowledge of the Vicsek model, we present a major update of its phase diagram in two space dimensions, summarizing comprehensive numerical simulations at length- and timescales never explored before. Our main conclusions are that multiple phase separation scenarios are at play, not just the simple microphase separation put forward in [Phys. Rev. Lett. 114, 068101 (2015)], and that the coexistence phase is subdivided in two. We also map out the region of metastability of the homogeneous Toner-Tu liquid phase.

papers.title: Coexistence phase of the two-dimensional Vicsek model
papers.summary: The Vicsek model continues to be central in statistical physics studies of active matter, with major recent surprises such as the partial metastability of the famous Toner-Tu flocking phase. Here we report on the diversity of band patterns observed in its coexistence phase --some of them never observed before--, but we also argue that most disappear in the infinite-size limit, leaving nevertheless a different picture than anticipated previously. We finally show that these rather regular, globally ordered band configurations can be destroyed by a localized perturbation: the coexistence phase is also at least partially metastable, and thus must be, asymptotically, a disordered phase made of a variety of chaotically interacting traveling bands.

papers.title: Exact cost of the Euclidean Maximum Traveling Salesman Problem in one dimension
papers.summary: We study the random Euclidean Maximum Traveling Salesman Problem: finding a Hamiltonian cycle of maximal total cost through any set of $N$ cities on a line, where each edge cost is a function of its Euclidean length. We characterize the maximizing cycles for convex increasing, concave increasing, and convex decreasing cost functions. For points sampled independently and uniformly from the unit interval, we derive explicit expressions for the average maximal cost for arbitrary $N$ and asymptotic expansions with power-law edge costs.

papers.title: Tunable annealing of defects in self-aligning active crystals
papers.summary: Obtaining defect-free single-crystals is of crucial importance in soft matter and materials science, spanning both fundamental interests and practical applications. Active crystals, encompassing diverse dense systems from living organisms to artificial metamaterials, can offer a promising platform for autonomous structural reorganization. We demonstrate that increasing spatiotemporal orientational fluctuations around the mean polarized state can enhance crystallographic order in active crystals. Poly-to-single-crystal transformations in defect-rich, self-aligned active Brownian crystals with coupled translational-rotational dynamics are investigated. We show that long-lived persistence with slow alignment controls the defect-annealing capability. By disentangling activity magnitude from associated timescales, we reveal activity-assisted annealing. Tuning the persistence length enables overcoming thermal energy barriers. Simultaneously adjusting persistence and alignment timescales can tune relaxation from `fast' to `slow', yielding defect-rich and defect-free crystals, respectively. Furthermore, active crystals of point particles are found to exhibit similar defect annealing when flocking is delayed by tuning the timescale of the velocity relaxation towards the polarized state. These findings suggest that the mechanism may extend to a broader class of active crystals. Our results intersect statistical physics of living soft matter with the mechanics of defects and microstructures, proposing a nonequilibrium route towards reconfigurable materials.

papers.title: Systemic collapse emergence from climate-induced perturbations in transportation networks
papers.summary: The interaction between human infrastructures and external events results in loss of functionality or even complete system disruption through a snowball effect of cascading-failures. Their complex interplay challenges their prevention, affecting the human population that rely on their functionality. Understanding how these networks respond to external perturbations is crucial for predicting and mitigating the impacts of disruptive events. In particular, meteorological events, while not preventable, can have significant impacts on human infrastructure. Here, we propose a model coupling the dynamics of transportation systems to the dynamics of external events considered as fields, to capture at the same time the critical behavior of the former and the level of influence of the latter. The impact of rainfalls on real-world railway networks provides a compelling case study, showcasing local endemic and system-wide disruptions around a critical value of the rainfall strength. Remarkably, localized perturbations on the wider network reveals the local weaknesses of the global infrastructure, and we assess them in terms of system perturbability and corresponding societal risk. Our framework opens the door to the quantitative analysis of criticalities in essential human infrastructure imputable to vulnerabilities that are set to intensify due to climate change.

papers.title: An infinite sequence of higher order Ehrenfest transitions in a one-dimensional crystal
papers.summary: Higher-order Ehrenfest phase transitions are exceptionally rare and poorly understood. We present an exactly solvable one-dimensional model exhibiting a sequence of Ehrenfest transitions of arbitrary $n\geq2$ order. These transitions occur without symmetry breaking and even the second-order transition lacks conventional critical behavior, although the density derivative of the correlation length diverges. Our results reveal a distinct class of noncritical phase transitions and help clarify the scope of the Ehrenfest classification.

papers.title: Origins of Faceted Anomalous Scaling
papers.summary: Fluctuating interfaces are typically characterized by their global, spectral, and local roughness exponents. Faceted anomalous scaling, characterized by $α_s>1$, $α_s\neqα$, and $α_{\mathrm{loc}}=1$, owes its name to the tendency of such interfaces to develop long, nearly linear segments called facets. Its statistical origin, and whether facets are required, have remained unclear. We show that this exponent structure is determined by the spatial statistics of the slope field. Slope increments split into typical fluctuations and rare, larger jumps. This anomalous scaling arises either when the typical slope increment displays genuine system-size-dependent anomalous scaling or when the rare jumps dominate the second moment. The two contributions can coexist, and their competition leads to bifractal scaling of the slopes. We establish this framework analytically in the generalized anharmonic Larkin model and the columnar Kardar--Parisi--Zhang equation, and we derive exactly the global, spectral, and local roughness exponents in both cases. The Larkin model realizes both mechanisms and produces anomalous interfaces with or without facets, whereas columnar KPZ belongs to the jump-dominated case and yields $α_s=3/2$.

papers.title: Fate of Arnold tongues and canards in Mobius systems with noise
papers.summary: We consider a class of noisy dynamical systems on the two-dimensional torus whose phase evolution is governed by Mobius transformations. In the deterministic limit, these systems favor phase-locking that is described by the band-gap structure of an associated Schrodinger equation with a periodic potential. We use the Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin method to characterize this structure in the slow-fast limit. Then we show that large-deviation theory describes fluctuations of the finite-time rotation number, whereas weak-noise escape actions determine the exponential scale of rare phase slips. These estimates provide quantitative criteria for metastable phase-locking and melting of Arnold tongues over a prescribed observation time. We derive sufficient conditions for stochastic trajectories to follow prescribed canard segments. With controlled entrance errors, exponential amplification of fluctuations along repelling branches leads to an exponentially small sufficient noise scale for canard persistence in the slow-forcing limit.

papers.title: High-order resonances and emergent coherent dynamics in interacting Stark chains
papers.summary: A linear potential gradient can strongly suppress quantum dynamics, while interactions can activate resonant many-body processes whose higher-order structure remains largely unexplored. Here we uncover a systematic hierarchy of high-order interaction--tilt resonances in an interacting Stark chain, where the resonance order counts the minimal number of elementary exchange steps involved. These resonances manifest as long-lived coherent oscillations with order-dependent timescales. By isolating individual resonant channels and developing a microscopic effective description, we connect these dynamical timescales to the underlying many-body exchange processes and reveal a pronounced dependence on the initial-state structure. Our results provide crucial insights into high-order many-body resonances and show how commensurate interaction-to-tilt ratios generate a hierarchy of parametrically slow coherent many-body dynamics.

papers.title: Poisson-shot-noise induced escape dynamics of a passive particle and a dimer
papers.summary: Mean First Passage Time (MFPT) is a crucial quantity that characterizes stochastic processes in various stochastic dynamical systems across different disciplines. The inverse of the MFPT, known as the escape rate, is helpful in the context of Brownian motion and chemical processes. The MFPT dynamics of a passive particle in the presence of active noises presents a fascinating avenue. In this work, we study the dynamics of two different systems: first, a single Brownian particle and second, a dimer (two Brownian particles connected by a spring). In both cases, the systems are kept in contact with a thermal bath and an active bath, and are trapped in a bistable potential. The active bath produces kicks that follow the Poisson distribution. The MFPT of the particle and the dimer is investigated in various scenarios. Analytical results are presented for the small kick variance approximation only. In this approximation, we formulate the MFPT in two scaling regimes: a weak-noise regime characterized by classical Arrhenius scaling for escape rate and a strong-noise regime in which the MFPT scales as a power law in the effective noise strength. For the general case, the problem is solved numerically. Next, under the same approximation, the MFPT of a dimer in the small-bond-strength regime is studied using a sequential-hopping mechanism, and in the large-bond-strength regime, the MFPT is formulated using the adiabatic elimination approach. Motivated by recent studies on speeding up the escape mechanism, the MFPT of the particle and the dimer in the presence of an intermediate barrier is also examined. We deduced from the numerical results that the MFPT can be enhanced and further optimized by selecting a suitable intermediate potential profile.

papers.title: Universal Quantum Criticality from a Gaussian Variational Manifold
papers.summary: Universal behavior at continuous phase transitions is encoded in long-wavelength fixed-point theories controlled by dimensionality and symmetries. It is a central question for which systems this universal behavior and the underlying long-wavelength description can be captured by a noninteracting theory allowing for analytical and accurate predictions. In this work we provide a systematic procedure for obtaining the best noninteracting fermionic description of a quantum phase transition through fermionic Gaussian states. We demonstrate the performance of our procedure for the interacting long-range transverse-field Ising chain. This formulation reduces the problem to a self-consistent Euler equation that yields a critical line in close agreement with independent numerical benchmarks, while its singular momentum structure provides analytic predictions for continuously varying critical properties. Yet exact diagonalization shows that Gaussian-state fidelity to the exact ground state is poorest, and non-Gaussianity strongest, near the transition. Thus, accurate predictions for critical properties can emerge from the Gaussian variational description even where its microscopic wave-function approximation is weakest.

papers.title: The resource cost of cooperative invasion
papers.summary: A contact network can favor cooperation by sheltering a lineage until its descendants compete with defectors as a group. We determine the contact strengths, invasion times and measurement effort needed to realize this advantage at fixed population size. Individuals reproduce according to averaged cooperation payoffs, and offspring replace neighbors through contacts of equal weight in both directions. Contact contrast is the ratio of strongest to weakest contact. Under weak selection on a six-site path, the least contrast needed to favor a single cooperator over the reverse invasion by a defector grows as $656ε^{-2}$ for uniformly placed mutants and $4050ε^{-3}$ for mutations in newborn offspring, as the benefit-cost ratio $b/c=1+ε$ approaches one. The extra power arises because rare replacement protects a site while suppressing mutation arrival there. Global bounds force two weakly coupled groups and exact mirror symmetry of the least-contrast contacts for sufficiently small $ε$. Under uniform introduction, additional contrast shortens the leading mean time to extinction or fixation in the absence of selection, from $12/ε$ toward $6/ε$ reproduction attempts, and eventually breaks the mirror symmetry of the fastest design. Estimating the uniform-introduction advantage from fixation outcomes of independent completed invasions defines a third optimum. Within the six-site family with mirror-symmetric, strongly separated contacts, we optimize contacts and selection strength with reproduction weighted linearly or exponentially by payoff. At fixed relative precision, with contrast a fixed factor above its minimum, the leading summed trial duration grows as $ε^{-3}$. Efficient measurement accepts a smaller advantage in exchange for shorter trials. The cheapest, fastest and most efficiently measured networks therefore differ.

papers.title: Quantum control as renormalization group flow
papers.summary: The Renormalization Group (RG) establishes relations between effective descriptions of physical systems at different scales; in Hamiltonian RG, these relations induce a flow in the space of Hamiltonians. In direct correspondence, we design an RG framework for quantum control by constructing a flow in the space of time-dependent Hamiltonians. A prescribed control subspace, selected to contain only experimentally accessible terms, forms the fixed-point manifold, while the flow preserves the target unitary and monotonically reduces the Hamiltonian weight outside this subspace. Exploiting the freedom in constructing the flow, we introduce flow-equation engineering to enhance the versatility of the framework for diverse control problems, including time-periodic and open-interval smooth protocols with prescribed endpoints. We provide two disparate applications to exhibit the utility of our approach: (i) Nonperturbative Floquet engineering beyond the regime of validity of high-frequency expansions, which we demonstrate by constructing an implementable time-periodic protocol for the Haldane model; (ii) Accessible fast-forward driving from unit-fidelity counterdiabatic evolution, which we showcase for large transverse-field Ising chains away from the adiabatic regime by compressing the long-range multibody adiabatic gauge potential into the original time-dependent Ising control schedules. Our control RG framework reveals a unifying perspective on Hamiltonian engineering and unitary quantum control, and can serve as an organizing principle behind seemingly disparate nonequilibrium quantum dynamics.

papers.title: Motility-Induced Phase Separation of Run-and-Tumble Particles under Local Stochastic Resetting
papers.summary: We investigate the non-equilibrium stationary states of a one-dimensional active gas composed of run-and-tumble particles (RTPs) undergoing motility-induced phase separation (MIPS) and subjected to local stochastic resetting at the origin. Unlike global resetting, local resetting maintains a mass-injection flux at the origin while preserving large-scale spatial self-organization. We demonstrate that above a critical resetting rate $r_c$, the active system undergoes a transition toward a stationary two-phase state featuring a dense liquid droplet centered at the origin coexisting with a surrounding gas phase. Using kinetic evolution equations, we derive the exact steady-state density profile expressed in terms of the Lambert function. The size of the droplet has a non-monotonic dependence on the resetting rate $r$, and attains its maximum. Furthermore, we analyze the dynamical stability of the supersaturated gas phase and show that a nucleated droplet relaxes exponentially toward its steady-state size with a relaxation timescale of $1/r$. We extend our framework to model a finite resetting velocity, proving that the stationary droplet size is invariant with respect to the resetting velocity.

papers.title: Generalised Fluctuating Dynamic Density-Functional Theory: Derivation and Applications
papers.summary: Classical density-functional theory is a powerful theoretical framework for studying the equilibrium density distribution of complex many-body systems. The core of the framework is to bridge microscopic and macroscopic descriptions of fluids through a variational principle that minimises the system's free energy. For dynamical settings, dynamic DFT (DDFT) extends the equilibrium framework to capture the time evolution of an order parameter, typically density. However, DDFT is often insufficient for mesoscopic systems far from equilibrium where fluctuations become significant, necessitating a stochastic extension: fluctuating DDFT. Here we derive a generalised FDDFT from first principles starting from the microscopic Hamiltonian dynamics using coarse-graining techniques, including Zwanzig's projection operator method. The resulting FDDFT applies to arbitrary observable fields, where the dynamics are driven by a thermodynamic force expressed in terms of an entropy functional. The dynamics consist of reversible, dissipative, and stochastic contributions, each directly linked to the underlying microscopic dynamics via the Liouville operator, Green-Kubo relations, and the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. To highlight the difference in the level of description between DDFT and FDDFT, we demonstrate how further coarse-graining via averaging leads to a generalised DDFT, valid at the macroscale. To showcase the effectiveness and utility of the generalised FDDFT, we apply it to two prototypical fluid systems: colloidal and simple viscous fluids. In the former case, we utilise the new formalism to re-derive the recently found colloidal FDDFT. In the latter case, we rigorously recover the non-isothermal extension of the Landau-Lifshitz fluctuating Navier-Stokes equations, providing fundamental derivation of this well-known phenomenological model, enabling to clarify its underlying principles.

papers.title: Gini coefficient of scientists and universities
papers.summary: Using the public database of Google Scholar article citations of scientists and universities we apply the algorithm for constructing Lorenz curves to the resulting citation distributions. Using Lorenz and Pareto curves, broadly used for economic analyses of wealth inequality across countries, we show that this approach gives a useful insight of citation distributions of world-leading scientists characterized by the Gini coefficient $G$ obtained from the Lorenz curves. For articles of 15 Nobel laureates (including A. Einstein and R. Feynman) we find the average $G=0.81$ with 50% of articles capturing only 2.7% of all citations and the top 10% (1%) of articles capturing 71% (30%) of all citations. Furthmore, we determine for world-leading universities the Gini coefficient via the citations of affiliated scientists. We show that about 65 percent of all citations belonging to a university (e.g. Princeton, Cambridge) are generated only by 10 percent of their university scientists while 50% of scientists produce only 3% of all university citations. The citation distributions are well described by the concept of Rayleigh-Jeans thermalization and condensation with similarities traced to the world wealth inequality.

papers.title: Chirality destroys oriented active solids
papers.summary: We construct a hydrodynamic theory of the effect of chiral and active force densities on three-dimensional uniaxial solids. We show that in a fixed background medium active chiral force densities---that arise at lower order in gradients than odd elasticity---generically destabilise the solid state. We further show this active instability also affects isotropic chiral solids in an anisotropic medium, a situation that is relevant for cell clusters moving through the extracellular matrix. Interestingly, the instability is eliminated in a higher-symmetry solid, known as the polar elastomer; indeed, we show that chirality does not affect the leading-order mechanics of such materials. We further demonstrate that momentum-conserving polar active solids have two chiral odd elasticities in contrast to the one discussed for two-dimensional solids. However, we again find that the higher symmetry of polar elastomers eliminates one of these with the remaining one being equivalent to the two-dimensional odd elastic force density. Our results should apply to numerous biological and condensed matter systems.

papers.title: Effect of chirality on active elastomers and solids in three dimensions
papers.summary: We examine the effect of chiral activity on nematic and polar uniaxial elastomers and solids by constructing the general hydrodynamic equations for these phases. We start with the elastomer, which is not only invariant under rigid rotations but also under an independent rotation of the uniaxial direction, and show that this higher symmetry strongly constrains the effects of chiral activity. We then break the elastomeric symmetry by adding a symmetry-breaking term to the free energy but still retain invariance under rigid rotations. The resulting state has the symmetry of a uniaxial solid, and we show that in a fixed background medium chiral activity generically destabilises it. The force density responsible for this {instability} vanishes as the field that breaks the elastomeric symmetry goes to zero. Further, the presence of the symmetry-breaking field also allows for an additional odd elastic force density that generically destabilises momentum-conserved chiral and uniaxial solids in the inertial regime.

papers.title: The long-range Ising CFT: perturbative and nonperturbative approaches
papers.summary: The long-range Ising model is the prototype of criticality with power-law interactions. In each dimension its interacting critical points form a one-parameter family of nonlocal conformal field theories, weakly coupled at both ends but not in between. We study this family in one, two and three dimensions from several independent directions. We extend the expansion about the generalized free field from three to eight loops and expand about the short-range end. We show that Hamiltonian truncation applies to this nonlocal theory once a truncation artifact is corrected. Where they can be compared, the resummed expansions, Hamiltonian truncation, the numerical renormalization group and Monte Carlo simulations agree on the dimension of the leading $\mathbb{Z}_2$-even scalar at the sub-percent level, as universality requires.

papers.title: Phase transitions of the antiferromagnetic $J_1$-$J_2$-$J_3$ Ising model on the cubic lattice
papers.summary: Motivated by the conflicting findings in prior studies regarding the nature of the phase transition for the three-dimensional antiferromagnetic $J_1$-$J_2$-$J_3$ Ising model on the cubic lattice with $J_1 = J_2 = J_3 = 1.0$, in this study we conduct a detailed investigation of this model using both Monte Carlo simulations and neural networks (NN). Here $J_1$ and $J_2$ are the intralayer nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor couplings, respectively, and $J_3$ is the nearest-neighbor interlayer interaction. By investigating the data obtained from much larger lattices than those used in previous studies, we find that the phase transition for $J_1 = J_2 = J_3 = 1.0$ is second order without any ambiguity. Hence we bring a resolution to this debate. Apart from $J_1 = J_2 = J_3 = 1.0$, we study the critical phenomenon associated with $J_2/J_1 = 4/7$ and $J_3 = J_1 = 1.0$ as well. In addition, by employing a dedicated training and testing strategy, our NN computation not only is much more efficient than those utilizing the standard procedures commonly used in the literature, but also requires only a per-mille fraction of the storage capacity needed by a conventional NN calculation when a large linear system size $L$ is considered. The method employed here provides an extremely resource-efficient route for applying NN techniques to study the critical behaviors of higher-dimensional systems.

papers.title: Subsystem quantum Rényi-Bhattacharyya distance in 2D CFTs and its holographic applications
papers.summary: We develop a systematic method to compute the subsystem fidelity and Rényi fidelity in two-dimensional conformal field theories (CFTs) from the operator product expansion of twist operators, and apply it to the subsystem quantum Bhattacharyya distance (BD) and Rényi-Bhattacharyya distance (RBD). We validate the method against exact results in the free massless fermion and boson theories, and then use it to compute the BD and RBD in holographic CFTs between two heavy primary states, between two thermal states, and between a heavy primary state and a thermal state. When the two states differ in their classical, order-$c$ data, the distances are of order $c$, and the states are distinguishable already at the level of classical gravity; when the leading data coincide, the distances are of order $1/c$ at every order of the short interval expansion, so that the distinguishability becomes a perturbative quantum gravity effect. For a heavy primary state and its thermal counterpart, the leading contribution to the BD appears at order $\ell^8$ and is of order $c^0$, whereas the RBD is generically of order $c$, in line with the earlier finding that a heavy primary state and a thermal state share the same order-$c$ entanglement entropy but have different order-$c$ Rényi entropies in the short interval expansion.

papers.title: Signatures of slow particle transport in the interacting Aubry-André chain
papers.summary: Slow delocalization in strongly disordered many-body quantum chains can originate from two distinct mechanisms: rare resonances and avalanches, rooted in the energy statistics, or an energy-independent combinatorial path-entropy obstruction in operator space. Quasiperiodic potentials eliminate rare regions with similar potentials that are thought to be responsible for avalanche instabilities and modify the statistics of resonances, thus allowing us to delineate the two mechanisms. To do so, we numerically study the entanglement entropy $S(t)$, number entropy $S_N(t)$, and Hartley number entropy $S_H(t)$ following a quantum quench in the interacting Aubry-André chain with disorder strength $D$. We find $S(t)\simμ\ln t$, $S_N(t)\simν\ln\ln t$ with growth rates $μ\simν\sim D^{-γ}$ and $γ\approx 3$, the same behavior that was previously found in the case of quenched disorder. Furthermore, the saturation values $S_H(t\to\infty)$ continue to grow with system size $L$ as $\ln L$, a growth that persists for $D\gtrsim 8$ where MBL was argued to be stable. The similarity of the quasi-periodic and quenched disorder cases points to a common origin of the slow particle transport that does not rely on rare-region avalanches and persists despite strongly modified resonance statistics.

papers.title: Generation of $N$-particle kappa-distributed velocities via superstatistical Gibbs sampling
papers.summary: The \emph{kappa} distribution is widely used to model heavy-tailed, non-equilibrium velocity distributions in space and laboratory plasmas. Its correct use in particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations requires more than sampling the single-particle marginal: the $N$-particle \emph{kappa} distribution predicts non-trivial correlations between the kinetic energies of particles. Building on the superstatistical structure, we implement a Gibbs sampler whose stationary distribution is the joint distribution of the velocities and $β$, so that the sampled velocities follow the $N$-particle \emph{kappa} distribution and reproduce these correlations by construction.

papers.title: Tensor network Monte Carlo study of the J1-J2 Ising model on the square lattice
papers.summary: The frustrated square-lattice J1-J2 Ising model exhibits rich magnetic phases, yet its phase transitions remain difficult to characterize due to critical slowing down in conventional Monte Carlo and truncation errors inherent to tensor renormalization group methods.We develop a tensor-network Monte Carlo (TNMC) algorithm for this frustrated model, which supports both open and periodic boundary conditions. For periodic lattices, we use a sweeping block-update strategy that updates spin blocks while fixing surrounding spins.To boost efficiency, we couple our sampler with histogram reweighting, and test each technique standalone to validate these independent optimizations.We perform extensive finite-size scaling analyses at g=0.55 and g=1.0, extracting apparent critical temperatures and effective thermal exponents from Binder-cumulant data.Our method offers an efficient, nearly bias-free path for large-scale simulations of J1-J2-type frustrated magnets under periodic boundaries and generalizes readily to other frustrated spin lattices.

papers.title: Emergent Sparsity: How Many Effective Variables Survive Coarse-Graining in AlphaEarth Embeddings?
papers.summary: AlphaEarth encodes each 10 m land pixel as a 64-component vector intended to support diverse global mapping tasks. Yet many scientific applications work at coarser spatial supports, for which fewer than 64 effective variables may suffice. We ask whether these vectors can be reorganized into ranked global nonlinear coordinates, how many suffice at a chosen reconstruction accuracy, and whether that number decreases with spatial scale. We thus describe effective dimension as a two-control surface over tolerance and spatial scale, rather than one intrinsic number. At each scale, a $β$-VAE scan with a common architecture produces a rank--distortion envelope, giving the smallest retained count achieved within the scanned family at each reconstruction tolerance. At 3% validation tolerance, this number falls from 24 to 7 when the scale is increased from 10 m to 78.9 km, whereas the corresponding PCA rank falls only from 46 to 38. Repeating the analysis on unit-norm targets preserves this trend.

papers.title: Enhancement of liquid-liquid phase transition under shear flow
papers.summary: In a liquid--liquid transition (LLT), a single-component liquid transforms into another liquid with different density and viscosity. Flow therefore couples to the transition, but the effect of shear flow is not understood. Here we investigate the LLT under shear with a two-order-parameter hydrodynamic model in which the viscosity depends on the non-conserved structural order parameter. Under shear, a fluctuation of the order parameter drives a compressional flow through the viscosity, and the resulting density change enhances the order parameter fluctuation. In a linear analysis, this feedback destabilizes the metastable liquid above a critical shear rate $\dotγ_{\rm c}$ for wavevectors in particular directions. Because the flow rotates the wavevector, a fluctuation grows only for a finite time duration, and its amplification is determined by the dimensionless shear rate $\dotγ/\dotγ_{\rm c}$ and the second dimensionless number $Λ$, the ratio of the thermodynamic relaxation rate of the order parameter to $\dotγ_{\rm c}$. In hydrodynamic simulations, shear above about $\dotγ_{\rm c}$ induces the transition in the metastable region when $Λ\gtrsim1$. The transition proceeds by nucleation of domains whose morphology becomes anisotropic. The incubation time decreases and the onset of the viscosity increase is accelerated as $\dotγ$ and $Λ$ increase. These results imply that the shear rate is a control variable of LLT in addition to temperature and pressure, selecting whether and how a metastable liquid transforms.

papers.title: Annealing Dynamics of the Two-Dimensional Fully Frustrated Ising Model
papers.summary: We study the dynamical scaling properties of the two-dimensional fully frustrated Ising model by simulated annealing. The model has a highly degenerate, critical ground state with well known equilibrium properties. To study its out-of-equilibrium behavior, we develop an annealing protocol that is convenient for extending the Kibble-Zurek mechanism to the case of an exponentially divergent correlation length in the limit of the temperature $T \to T_c = 0$. We find excellent agreement with the scaling forms derived, including a dependence on the initial temperature that is not present in the conventional Kibble-Zurek mechanism. The dynamic exponent $z$ is consistent among all quantities studied; fits of its dependence on the initial temperature give $z = 1.99(2)$ (susceptibility), $z = 2.072(8)$ (excess energy), and $z = 2.09(3)$ (Edwards-Anderson order parameter). These values are close to $z=2$, which is consistent with previous studies of relaxation after instantaneous quenches and of time dependent correlations in equilibrium, including the estimate $z = 2.004(9)$ from equilibrium autocorrelation functions.

papers.title: Generative marginal learning for finite-size molecular simulation with application to stress calculation
papers.summary: We propose generative marginal learning (GML), a framework for equilibrium sampling and local observable estimation in molecular simulations. By training a conditional diffusion model on large-system simulations, GML learns the marginal distribution of a retained region, enabling configuration generation without explicitly simulating the surrounding environment or imposing periodic boundary conditions on the retained region. We derive a marginal effective potential and the associated conditional mean-force identity, which provide the basis for both denoising and force-alignment training. As an application, we estimate the spatially averaged Irving--Kirkwood stress near a vacancy defect. Numerical results demonstrate that GML substantially improves pair structure and local stress accuracy compared with small periodic molecular dynamics simulations, mitigating finite-size effects in calculating local molecular observables.

papers.title: The Ericson Transition in Time-Reversal Invariant Systems: Orthogonally Invariant Hamiltonians
papers.summary: We investigate the distributions of off-diagonal scattering matrix elements and cross-sections in the Ericson regime for systems that are time-reversal and rotationally invariant. In previous works, we developed techniques to analyze the Ericson transition by means of asymptotic expansions in the cases of unitarily and symplectically invariant Hamiltonians. Here, we prove that Gaussian and exponential behavior is found as the leading-order term of an asymptotic expansion of those distributions also in the orthogonal case, which is often the relevant one for analyzing experiments. Moreover, we derive the subleading-order term and compare with numerical simulations. Finally, we discuss similarities and differences of the Ericson transition for all three Wigner-Dyson classes.

papers.title: Large Deviations in Switching Diffusion: Dynamical Condensation and Diffusivity BBP Transition
papers.summary: We consider a Brownian particle with position $x(t)$ whose diffusivity changes at Poissonian switching times, with each new value drawn independently from a bounded distribution $W(D)$. Assuming $W(D)\sim C(D_{\max}-D)^ν$ near its upper edge, we study the large-deviation regime $x(t)\simeq yt$ with $y = O(1)$ at large times, far beyond the typical diffusive scale. In a recent work Guéneau et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 067102 (2025), the rate function of the displacement was obtained through a renewal approach and it was shown to display several singularities. In this paper, we carry out a detailed study of the corresponding dynamical phase transitions and trajectory condensation. For moderate $y$, the imposed displacement is shared among $O(t)$ displacement increments accumulated during successive intervals between switches. Beyond a first threshold $y_-$, one interval produces an increment of order $t$ carrying a finite fraction of the total displacement, signaling dynamical condensation. For $ν>1$, a second threshold $y_+>y_-$ is reached when this macroscopic increment carries asymptotically the entire imposed displacement, whereas for $0<ν\leq1$ the two thresholds merge, $y_-=y_+$. In turn, the moment-generating function of $x(t)$ displays a complementary transition from collective contributions of many diffusivities to selection of states near $D_{\max}$. We show that this transition is governed by the same edge mechanism as the Baik-Ben Arous-Péché (BBP) transition, indicating that diffusivity selection and trajectory condensation are two manifestations of the same phenomenon. We validate our predictions for the dynamical condensation against numerical results from rare event sampling.

papers.title: Run-and-tumble particles in a harmonic external field: constructing the solution of the Fokker-Planck equation from the equations of motion
papers.summary: A method for integrating the Langevin equations of motion for run-and-tumble particles is introduced to compute the joint distribution of their position and active velocity, with and without a harmonic external force field. The key step is the construction of the moments of the distribution and the correlation functions, conditional on the particles being in a specific state at the final time. For one-dimensional run-and-tumble particles in a harmonic external potential, the exact steady-state distributions for the tumble state, as well as for the run state conditional on a specified velocity direction, are obtained. This enables us to demonstrate their equivalence to the exact solutions of the corresponding Fokker-Planck equations.

papers.title: Three-body corrections to Brownian hard-sphere viscosity
papers.summary: For Brownian hard spheres without hydrodynamic interactions, we obtain a conditional enclosure between 1.8266948 and 1.8267157 for the third-order zero-shear Brownian viscosity coefficient. It applies when the physical three-body correction coincides with the finite-energy weak solution and the remote remainder in the pair adjoint identity vanishes. Kirkwood superposition gives zero because three nonzero pair contributions cancel exactly. An elementary radial identity exposes this cancellation, and a common contact-stress convention allows direct comparison of closure predictions. Although superposition solves the bulk equation, it leaves a shared-contact flux error. Correcting this error defines a unique weak response with positive Dirichlet energy. Explicit symmetric trials yield a variational lower bound and a residual upper bound using the rotational structure of shear and three-sphere geometry. Exact integration and outward interval evaluation enclose the fixed-trial functionals. Under the stated physical conditions, the resulting interval excludes all closure coefficients compared here and supplies a quantitative benchmark for dilute three-body Brownian stress.

papers.title: Scaling Dimensions and Two-Point Amplitudes from Operator Covariance Matrices
papers.summary: The long distance behavior of two-point functions of critical lattice statistical mechanics models depend on detailed information of the underlying quantum field theory. Yet these universal properties can be difficult to extract because generic lattice operators couple to the infinite hierarchy of continuum scaling operators with unknown coefficients. Recently in Physical Review E 114, 024146 (2026), one approach to disentangle some of this information was proposed using the eigen-decomposition of the operator covariance matrix constructed from cross correlations of a finite set of $N_\ell$ lattice operators. In this work we analyze this method in detail. We provide an explicit proof that under the assumption of scale invariance the leading decay of the eigenvalues are controlled by the smallest $N_\ell$ scaling dimensions, even after taking irrelevant perturbations into account. Based on this understanding, we propose a new method by which the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix can be used to construct the amplitudes of the continuum two-point correlation functions. This allows for a complete determination of the structure of the continuum two-point functions from the lattice covariance matrix. We demonstrate our ideas both on synthetic data sets (drawn from the scaling hypothesis) and numerically exact data for the two dimensional Ising model.

papers.title: Frustration and topology in the phase behavior of solute-frustrated $q$-clock models
papers.summary: Frustration can enhance fluctuations and create new and interesting phase behavior. When combined with the ability to host topological defects, frustration can increase the complexity of a system's phase diagram through topological and frustrated topological transitions. To understand the interplay of frustration and topology on phase behavior, we introduce and study solute-frustrated $q$-clock (SF$q$C) models, in which solute sites are added to the $q$-clock model, a lattice model where each spin can take one of $q$ orientations. The $q$-clock model can exhibit spontaneous symmetry breaking and topological transitions, and the interaction between the spins and a solute frustrates the system, in essence by creating a fixed lower bound on the concentration of positive topological defects or vortices. We perform Monte Carlo simulations and develop theoretical descriptions of SF$q$C models with $q=4$ and $q=6$ to understand their phase behavior. We find that these systems exhibit rich phase diagrams that depend on the choice of parameters. In particular, SF$q$C models have a wide range of interesting low-temperature phases, including the presence of strongly frustrated domains and the absence of long-range order. We also find topological effects even at low temperatures; for instance, we find that topological defects can drive crystallization. We anticipate these results to guide the development of materials that take advantage of frustration and topology to tune phase behavior and fluctuations.

papers.title: Spontaneous particle-hole symmetry breaking in a disordered two-site quantum breakdown model
papers.summary: We study spontaneous particle-hole symmetry breaking in a disordered two-site quantum breakdown model. The model is solvable in the limit of a large number of fermionic modes on each site. For a small ratio of the numbers of modes on the two sites, we derive the free energy analytically and find a finite-temperature symmetry-breaking transition. This transition changes from continuous to first order as the number of fermions produced in each conversion increases. Numerical results show that both types of transition persist beyond this regime, with an order-parameter exponent close to $1/2$ for continuous transitions.

papers.title: Autonomous Thermal Switching Outperforms the Frozen Optimum with Vanishing Correlations
papers.summary: Can autonomous thermal switching outperform the best frozen barrier allocation while keeping system--auxiliary correlations arbitrarily small? We establish this relaxation advantage at fixed lowering budget and visible equilibrium, preserving joint detailed balance. On finite reversible networks, optimal fast switching mixes profiles concentrating the budget on single edges. A three-state model gives a strict gain and its finite-rate threshold. Faster switching preserves the gain while correlations vanish throughout relaxation. Collective and continuous models suggest a colloidal test.

papers.title: Energy-optimal scheduling for clocked reversible computing
papers.summary: Computational dissipation may arise from both information erasure and finite-time operation, although both contributions can in principle be avoided in the absence of space and time constraints. Logically reversible computation can replace erasure with ancilla cleanup, and slow adiabatic protocols can eliminate any excess finite-time dissipation. Under limited memory and in finite time, however, choosing reversible cleanup over erasure requires additional dissipative operations, creating a semi-reversible energy--memory--time tradeoff. We formulate this tradeoff at a fixed operating point of an externally clocked thermally coupled computer, where reversible checkpoint moves and local irreversible erasures have specified effective prices $ε_R$ and $ε_I$. Their ratio $λ=ε_I/ε_R$ selects an energy-optimal semi-reversible schedule under a checkpoint-memory bound by trading reversible moves against erasures. For a sequential computation whose dependency graph is a line, we derive an exact separator recurrence and prove that an asymptotically optimal schedule repeats a strictly reversible block followed by one local erasure. Coupling this scheduling theorem to a stochastic-thermodynamic constitutive model shows how temperature, primitive duration, memory, and device-dependent operation costs determine whether the optimal schedule uses reversible cleanup, elective erasures, or erasure at every disposal.

papers.title: Beyond low-dissipation regime: general condition for Curzon-Ahlborn efficiency
papers.summary: In recent years, physicists have extensively investigated the universality of Curzon-Ahlborn (CA) efficiency as the efficiency at maximum power of heat engines, which, like Carnot efficiency, is determined only by heat-bath temperatures. While the universality of the CA efficiency to the first order in the temperature difference is established within linear response theory in the inverse operation time, it is generally lost at quadratic order. In the low-dissipation Carnot heat engine model known as the standard framework, the symmetric dissipation condition is necessary. Yet, it is not a necessary condition as the original CA model that adopts endoreversibility does not require such symmetry. In this study, we extend the low-dissipation model to include nonlinear response in the inverse operation time and derive a general condition under which the CA efficiency is recovered in the quadratic order. The generalized symmetric dissipation condition and the CA model with Newton's law of cooling are shown to be special cases of this condition. By applying the obtained condition, we also clarify the condition under which an endoreversible model with a general heat-transfer law exhibits the CA efficiency.

papers.title: Microphase Separation and Ionic Aggregation in Oppositely Charged End-Functionalized Polymer Blends
papers.summary: We study the phase behavior of binary blends of polymers with oppositely charged termini using an ion-correlation-augmented self-consistent field theory (IC-SCFT). Under the low dielectric conditions typical for organic polymer melts, strong ion correlations drive association of multiple chain ends, leading to emergent multichain architectures that go beyond a simple ion-paired diblock copolymer picture previously used to interpret recent experiments. At moderate to strong polymer segregation, the resulting phase diagram differs considerably from this effective-diblock prediction: ion clustering broadens the lamellar and cylindrical windows while suppressing the network phases, the reverse of the trend for end-charged diblock copolymers. At weak segregation, the two polymers remain miscible even as ion clustering persists, and decreasing chain length drives the clusters themselves through a sphere-to-cylinder-to-lamella shape transition, connecting continuously to the aggregation behavior of classical terminally charged ionomers in the limit when one of the polymer species shrinks to just the charged end. These results reveal that ion clustering -- beyond simple pairwise bonding -- shapes the self-assembly of end-charged polymer blends.

papers.title: Maximum-Temperature Theorem for a Nanothermometer
papers.summary: The steady-state temperature predicted for an ideal point heat source diverges in conventional heat-conduction theory, but no physical thermometer measures a point value. We derive a sharp, shape-independent upper bound on the quasi-steady temperature rise of a sensor with thermometric volume $V_\mathrm{s}$, placed anywhere inside a region enclosed by an isothermal reference surface. The bound requires only the total heat power generated in the region $\dot{Q}$, a lower bound on its thermal conductivity $κ_\mathrm{m}$, and the value of $V_\mathrm{s}$. It is otherwise independent of the heat-source distribution, domain shape, and source--sensor distance. For $\dot{Q}=50~\mathrm{pW}$, $κ_\mathrm{m} = 0.1~\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $V_\mathrm{s}=10^{-22}\mathrm{\,m^3}$, approximately the volume of a $60~\mathrm{nm}$-diameter sphere, the theorem permits a maximum temperature rise of approximately $2~\mathrm{mK}$ above the reference level. The result applies directly to nanodiamonds, upconversion nanoparticles, fluorescent polymer particles, and core-shell quantum dots. It shows that neither source localization nor uncertain source-sensor separation can account for kelvin-scale readings under steady-state heat conduction.

papers.title: Encoding Hyperuniformity in Geometric Networks: Structural Signatures and Diffusion Dynamics
papers.summary: Disordered hyperuniformity is a recently discovered exotic state exhibiting anomalously suppressed density fluctuations at long wavelengths, and its generalization to network systems remains an important open question. Here, we show that, across a wide range of systems, geometric networks retain substantially more long-wavelength density information from the underlying point configurations than Delaunay triangulations. Within geometric networks, hyperuniformity manifests as suppressed vertex-to-vertex fluctuations in a range of network structural observables, including closeness centrality, vertex strength, and eigenvector centrality. These measures not only distinguish hyperuniform networks from non-hyperuniform ones, but also separate near-hyperuniform configurations from hyperuniform systems with strong local disorder, solving a central challenge in network hyperuniformity. We connect these structural signatures to network dynamics by introducing a relaxation-time centrality based on diffusion and demonstrate that hyperuniform geometric networks exhibit more homogeneous relaxation behavior than non-hyperuniform geometric networks. These results reveal how the suppression of large-scale density fluctuations manifests in both network structure and diffusion dynamics.
